title: Machine Learning, Foundation Models, Skills, and Agents in the Energy Industry: A Systematic, Evidence-Graded Survey
content: Artificial intelligence in energy is reported far more often than it is deployed, and the evidence that would let an operator tell the difference is scattered across literatures that do not cite each other. This survey assembles it. We grade 678 claims drawn from 883 evidence cards over 455 sources across four pillars (classical and deep machine learning, foundation models, capability packaging and agents) and the whole value chain, applying one deployment ladder (demo, pilot, field trial and production) to every system. Three findings recur. First, the subfields differ in evaluation regime, not in any measured model capability: the earliest petroleum large-language-model benchmarks found date from 2026, the power sector’s from 2024, and none of them reports a human-expert baseline, so none of their scores can be read as expertlevel. Second, in this corpus, two places differ: in drilling automation and artificial lift, software writes setpoints to field equipment with no human approving each action, yet the artificial-lift system with the broadest such authority contains no machine learning, and every reinforcement-learning system here that actuates does so in a simulator, not on a well. Third, the sources in this corpus rarely measure the field’s own adoption: no Tier A source found reports an adoption rate, a pilot-to-production conversion ratio, a total cost of ownership, or a post-mortem of a cancelled programme, and 63 claims here are formally evidenced absences. The survey reports its own failures, among them a retracted absence claim, a measured skew in its own corpus and seven source caches holding the wrong document.
